core.title: Split any feature exceeding 2 new tables, 2 async jobs, or 2 integrations
core.given: A feature whose scope includes tables, async jobs, or integrations
core.when: The planner authors, revises, or reviews the feature, or finds during any phase that the feature is over-limit
core.then: If the feature has more than 2 new tables, more than 2 async jobs, or more than 2 integrations, split it so that every resulting feature stays within all three limits.
prefer: Split along the excess. Move the extra tables, jobs, or integrations into a separate feature with its own acceptance.
avoid: Leaving a feature that exceeds any one limit unsplit, or treating the limits as advisory.
Gaming the count, e.g. merging distinct jobs or tables into one, or wrapping several dependencies behind one facade.
Excluding existing jobs or integrations from the count. Only tables are limited to new ones.
core.why: Tables bring maintenance, schema-evolution, and performance cost. Async jobs bring operational complexity (monitoring, retry, inconsistency). Integrations bring external dependencies, security exposure, and failures you cannot control.
evidence: For every feature, the reviewer counts new tables, async jobs, and integrations and confirms each count is <= 2.
If the original scope exceeded any limit, the plan shows the split into features that each satisfy all three limits.
verification: Hard per-feature ceilings that force a split: new tables <= 2, async jobs <= 2, integrations <= 2. The comparison is inclusive: a count <= 2 passes, > 2 requires a split.
Each limit is checked independently: exceeding any one is a violation even when the other two are within bounds.
Count scope: only tables are qualified as 'new'; every async job and every integration the feature uses counts, whether new or already existing.
The rule has no phase restriction: a phase signal only routes an over-limit feature found during implementation or review back to the planner; it is not an exclusion.

Counting a feature's resources from plan prose is a judgement-based finding; a structured counter would be a new observer in the realizing stack, so verification otherwise relies on the reviewer's count.

fires: A planned feature introduces 3 new tables.
A feature uses 3 async jobs, even if some of them already exist.
A feature depends on 3 integrations, even if some of them are already wired up.
During implementation or review, a feature turns out to exceed one of the ceilings.
doesNotFire: A feature with exactly 2 new tables, 2 async jobs, and 2 integrations (the limit is not exceeded).
A feature that touches more than 2 existing tables but adds at most 2 new ones, and stays within the job and integration ceilings.

profileRequirements.meaning: The concrete plan-artifact kinds that declare a feature's scope, so the file_kind activation fact and the reviewer's count can be located in a stack.

neutralityNotes: The convention is a planner-scope constraint over resource kinds (tables, async jobs, integrations) and was already stack-neutral; the core names no stack, runtime, framework, path, or file suffix, so given/when/then/why/prefer/avoid/evidence and fires/doesNotFire carry over verbatim. Two ATDD-Bun words could not be neutralized: 'wagon' (task_term) and 'wagon manifest' (file_kind), the stack's local names for a bounded product slice and its plan artifact; both stay bunOnly, and the concrete plan-artifact kinds come from the profile via roles.plan_artifact.kinds. No profile key names a stack-local bounded-slice term, but the core does not need one: the neutral planning terms cover routing, so no key is proposed. The 2/2/2 ceilings and the 'new tables' qualifier are the convention's own normative content and stay in the core rather than becoming profile data; the source term id 'hard_limit' is a realization trace label kept bunOnly.
